section.title: Taste and See That the Lord Is Good
section.sectionRationale: An acrostic psalm of David blessing the LORD at all times, inviting others to taste and see His goodness, instructing children in the fear of the LORD, and closing with the promise that the LORD protects the righteous so completely that not one of their bones will be broken, words the Gospel of John identifies as fulfilled at the cross, John 19:36.
section.thesis: David's invitation to taste and see that the LORD is good, and his testimony that God is near to the brokenhearted and protects the righteous so that not one bone is broken, finds its fullest meaning in Jesus Christ, the true Passover Lamb whose bones remained unbroken at the cross.
section.frameNote: Six movements: blessing the LORD at all times (1-3); seeking the LORD and being answered, the angel of the LORD encamping around those who fear Him (4-7); the invitation to taste and see that the LORD is good (8-10); wisdom instruction for children in the fear of the LORD (11-14); the LORD's eyes on the righteous and nearness to the brokenhearted (15-18); and the closing promise of deliverance, unbroken bones, and redemption (19-22).

units.label: I will bless the LORD at all times

verses.text: I will bless the LORD at all times; His praise will always be on my lips.
My soul boasts in the LORD; let the oppressed hear and rejoice.
Magnify the LORD with me; let us exalt His name together.

units.label: The angel of the LORD encamps
units.note: seeking the LORD and being answered

verses.text: I sought the LORD, and He answered me; He delivered me from all my fears.
Those who look to Him are radiant with joy; their faces shall never be ashamed.
This {{ani|poor}} man called out, and the LORD heard him; He saved him from all his troubles.
The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear Him, and he delivers them.

units.label: Taste and see that the LORD is good
units.note: an invitation to experience God's goodness

verses.text: {{taam|Taste}} and see that the LORD is good; blessed is the man who takes refuge in Him!
Fear the LORD, you His saints, for those who fear Him lack nothing.
Young lions go lacking and hungry, but those who seek the LORD lack no good thing.
Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the LORD.
Who is the man who delights in life, who desires to see good days?
Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from deceitful speech.
Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it.

units.label: The LORD is near to the brokenhearted

verses.text: The eyes of the LORD are on the righteous, and His ears are inclined to their cry.
But the face of the LORD is against those who do evil, to wipe out all memory of them from the earth.
The righteous cry out, and the LORD hears; He delivers them from all their troubles.
The LORD is near to the brokenhearted; He saves the contrite in spirit.

units.label: Not one of them will be broken

verses.text: Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him from them all.
He protects all his bones; not one of them will be {{shabar|broken}}.
Evil will slay the wicked, and the haters of the righteous will be condemned.
The LORD redeems His servants, and none who take refuge in Him will be condemned.

ani.gloss: Poor, afflicted, lowly. David identifies himself with this term, not as a title of shame but as the honest condition from which the LORD hears and delivers, a pattern the Messiah Himself embraces, Isaiah 53:7, Luke 4:18.

taam.gloss: To taste, perceive, experience directly. David's invitation is not merely to believe facts about God's goodness but to experience it firsthand, an invitation echoed in 1 Peter 2:3, quoting this very verse of those who have tasted that the Lord is good.

shabar.gloss: To break, shatter. God's promise that not one bone of the righteous will be broken, verse 20, is quoted directly by John as fulfilled when soldiers found Jesus already dead and did not break His legs, John 19:33-36, echoing also the Passover lamb regulation, Exodus 12:46.

basic.context: David resolves to bless the LORD at all times, inviting the oppressed and all who hear to rejoice with him. He testifies that seeking the LORD brought deliverance from fear, and that the angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear Him. He invites everyone to taste and see the LORD's goodness for themselves, teaches children the fear of the LORD as the path to a good life, and describes God's nearness to the brokenhearted. The psalm closes celebrating that though the righteous suffer many afflictions, the LORD delivers them completely, even protecting their very bones from being broken, and redeems His servants from condemnation.
basic.hermeneutics: This acrostic psalm should be read as both personal testimony and wisdom instruction, moving naturally from praise, to invitation, to teaching, showing that experiential knowledge of God's goodness, not merely correct doctrine about Him, is what the psalm calls every reader to taste for themselves.
basic.originalLanguages: David identifies himself as ani, poor and afflicted, the honest condition from which the LORD delivers him, invites others to taam, taste, God's goodness directly rather than merely hearing about it, and closes promising that not one bone of the righteous will shabar, break, a promise John identifies as fulfilled at the cross, John 19:36.
basic.typology: David's identification as the poor and afflicted one whom the LORD hears anticipates the Messiah's own embrace of lowliness, Isaiah 53:7, Luke 4:18, and the promise that not one bone of the righteous will be broken, verse 20, anticipates both the Passover lamb regulation, Exodus 12:46, and its fulfillment in Jesus, whose legs were not broken at the crucifixion, John 19:33-36.
basic.christ: John explicitly quotes this psalm's promise, that not one bone of the righteous would be broken, as fulfilled when Roman soldiers, finding Jesus already dead, did not break His legs as they did the two criminals crucified with Him, John 19:33-36. This same detail echoes the Passover lamb, of which no bone was to be broken, Exodus 12:46, identifying Jesus as the true Passover Lamb whose sacrifice delivers His people. And where David invites others to taste and see the LORD's goodness, verse 8, Peter applies this directly to those who have tasted that the Lord is good in Christ, 1 Peter 2:3.
basic.god: God is shown as intimately near to the brokenhearted and contrite, attentive to the cries of the afflicted, and so thorough in His protection of the righteous that even their bones are kept from breaking, a promise of care extending to the smallest details of suffering.
basic.crossReferences: John 19:33-36 quotes this psalm's promise of unbroken bones as literally fulfilled at the crucifixion of Jesus. Exodus 12:46 commands that no bone of the Passover lamb be broken, a regulation John connects directly to Jesus as the true Passover Lamb. 1 Peter 2:3 quotes this psalm's invitation, 'you have tasted that the Lord is good,' applying it to believers' experience of Christ.
basic.oneStory: David's invitation to taste and see the LORD's goodness, and his testimony that God protects the righteous so completely that not one bone is broken, find their fullest meaning in Jesus Christ, the true Passover Lamb whose unbroken bones at the cross fulfill this very psalm, and in whom all who taste His goodness are redeemed from condemnation.

context.literary:
Psalm 34 is an alphabetic acrostic, and the alphabet is the frame on which its three voices are hung. It opens in the first person, 'I will bless the LORD', verses 1 to 3, and stays there through the testimony of verse 4, 'I sought the LORD, and He answered me.' Then something quiet happens. In verse 6 David steps outside himself and speaks of 'this poor man' in the third person, as though pointing at a stranger, and in verse 7 the whole company of 'those who fear Him' is in view. By verse 9 he is issuing commands to 'you His saints', and from verse 11 he is a teacher addressing 'children'. The movement is from one man's rescue, to a pattern any hearer can join, to a lesson that can be handed down. David makes himself the specimen and then the instructor.

The acrostic has two well known irregularities. The line that should begin with the letter waw is missing between verses 5 and 6, and after the last letter, tav, in verse 21 there is a further line, verse 22, beginning with pe, the letter that already began verse 16. That closing verse, 'The LORD redeems His servants', therefore sits outside the completed alphabet as a coda, and Psalm 25 ends the same way with its own extra pe line, 'Redeem Israel, O God, from all its distress', Psalm 25:22. Whether by design or by the accidents of transmission, the effect is that the alphabet is finished and redemption still has the last word.

A few threads run all the way through. The word 'all' keeps returning: all my fears, verse 4, all his troubles, verses 6 and 17, them all, verse 19, all his bones, verse 20. The psalm is also strikingly bodily, with lips and soul, faces, taste, tongue, eyes and ears, heart and spirit, and finally bones, so that the whole person is gathered into the praise, from the mouth that opens the psalm to the skeleton that closes its promise. The pivot of the poem is verse 11, 'Come, children, listen to me', which is exactly where the acrostic reaches lamed, the letter of learning and teaching in the alphabet's own sequence.
context.historical:
The superscription ties the psalm to the day David 'feigned madness before Abimelech', and the story is told in 1 Samuel 21:10-15. David has fled from Saul and reaches Achish, king of Gath, and Gath is Goliath's home town, a poor place to go carrying Goliath's own sword, 1 Samuel 21:9. The king's servants recognise him and quote the dance song, 'Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands', and David 'was very much afraid'. So he 'changed his behavior before them', scratching the doors and letting saliva run into his beard, and Achish sends him away with contempt: 'Am I in need of madmen?' The Bible's own footnote observes that Abimelech is another name for Achish, most naturally a royal title, as 'Pharaoh' was in Egypt.

What is remarkable is what the psalm leaves out. Nothing in it mentions the drooling, the gate, or the ruse. The escape that was won by a humiliating piece of acting is reported as pure gift: 'I sought the LORD, and He answered me.' The man who rescued himself, in the view of anyone at the gate, says he was rescued. Verse 5, 'their faces shall never be ashamed', reads differently against a scene where David had just made himself an object of ridicule in front of a foreign court.

What followed shows who the 'oppressed' of verse 2 might be. David left Gath for the cave of Adullam, and there 'all who were distressed or indebted or discontented rallied around him', about four hundred men, 1 Samuel 22:1-2. A psalm that begins 'let the oppressed hear and rejoice', and speaks of a poor man whom the LORD heard, would have found its first audience in a band of outcasts learning what their new leader had just learned.

The address to 'children' belongs to the household and the classroom. Israel was told to teach its sons the LORD's words, Deuteronomy 6:7, and the wisdom teachers of Proverbs open in just this voice, 'Listen, my sons', Proverbs 4:1. The acrostic form would have helped such a poem to be learned by heart.
context.canonical:
The psalm sits in a run of Book I poems about the LORD's watchful care. Psalm 33 ends by saying that 'the eyes of the LORD are on those who fear Him', to 'deliver them from death and keep them alive in famine', Psalm 33:18-19, and Psalm 34 takes that general claim and puts a face and a story to it. It shares its closing prayer word with Psalm 25, and its key verb of refuge with the whole Psalter's front door: Psalm 2 ends, 'Blessed are all who take refuge in Him', Psalm 2:12, and Psalm 34 both begins its invitation and ends its last verse with that same act of taking refuge, verses 8 and 22.

In the New Testament the psalm is quoted more than once. Peter, urging new believers to long for pure spiritual milk, says 'now that you have tasted that the Lord is good', 1 Peter 2:3, and he applies to Jesus a verse that in the psalm speaks of the LORD. Later in the same letter he quotes verses 12 to 16 at length, 'Whoever would love life and see good days must keep his tongue from evil', 1 Peter 3:10-12, and turns them into counsel for suffering Christians who must answer hostility with blessing. John reads the promise about the bones as a witness to the cross, John 19:36. The Bible's own footnotes flag these three citations.

The psalm's vocabulary also feeds the Beatitudes. The poor, the hungry, the peacemaker and the persecuted all have their counterparts in it, and Luke's Jesus says 'Blessed are you who hunger now, for you will be filled', Luke 6:21, in a voice that has clearly been listening to 'those who seek the LORD lack no good thing.' The New Testament does not treat the psalm as a museum piece but as a living script for how disciples live when the world is against them.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David meant his hearers to leave the psalm changed in three ways. First, he wanted them to praise with him, and not only as a mood but as a policy: 'at all times', which in his case included the hour at Gath when things looked worst. Praise that waits for good news is not what he is recommending.

Second, he wanted them to test God for themselves. 'Taste and see' is an invitation to try the LORD's goodness rather than to accept it on hearsay, and the evidence he offers is his own story, told in a way that lets any poor person see themselves in it. The first hearers, a scattered band of the desperate, were meant to draw the conclusion that the God who heard one poor man will hear them.

Third, he wanted to hand on a skill. 'I will teach you the fear of the LORD' is followed by a curriculum that is shockingly practical: guard your tongue, turn from evil, do good, pursue peace. The fear of the LORD is not dread but a whole way of life, and it begins with the mouth, the same organ that opened the psalm in praise. He also does not sell a painless life. Verse 19 states plainly that 'many are the afflictions of the righteous', so that the promise of deliverance is set inside an honest acknowledgment of trouble.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm mixes report, promise and command, and each needs to be read for what it is. The story behind it is description: David really was rescued, and the superscription anchors that. Verses such as 'those who fear Him lack nothing', verse 9, are statements of what God is like and how He deals with those who trust Him. They are not a contract that no believer will ever be hungry. The man who wrote them had begged consecrated bread from the priest at Nob only shortly before, 1 Samuel 21:1-6, and the psalm itself concedes many afflictions.

The same is true of 'not one of them will be broken'. It describes God's protective care, and it is not a guarantee that no faithful person will ever be injured or killed. Stephen was stoned, Acts 7:59, and the psalm's own author lived for years with a price on his head. The verse's fullest force comes when it is read with its fulfilment in John, where an unbroken body is still a pierced body.

The commands are different, and they carry forward directly. Taste and see, fear the LORD, keep your tongue from evil, turn away from evil and do good, seek peace and pursue it: Peter treats these as binding on Christians without any adjustment, 1 Peter 3:10-11. They are meant to be practised now, and the psalm's promises are what make them worth practising.

debates.question: How does John 19:36 use 'not one of them will be broken'? Is Psalm 34:20 a messianic prediction, a general promise fulfilled in Christ, or a pointer to the Passover regulation?

views.label: A direct prediction of the Messiah
views.case: John says 'these things happened so that the Scripture would be fulfilled', which he uses of events he sees as foretold. On this view the psalm's righteous sufferer is the Messiah and the verse is about His body specifically. The difficulty is that the psalm speaks in the plural of 'the righteous' and gives no hint of a single figure.

views.label: A general promise that finds its pattern in Christ
views.case: The verse belongs to the psalm's broad teaching that the LORD guards the righteous, and John sees Jesus as the perfectly righteous man in whom that pattern comes to its most literal fulfilment. This fits how the psalm was originally read and how the New Testament often uses the Psalms, as a script whose meaning is filled up in Christ.

views.label: An allusion to the Passover regulation, with the psalm as support
views.case: The exact wording John gives is a passive, 'will be broken', close to the psalm, but the idea that a sacrificial victim's bones must stay whole comes from Exodus 12:46 and Numbers 9:12. John's single citation may deliberately combine both texts so that the righteous sufferer of the psalm and the Passover lamb of Exodus meet in one man.

debates.bearing: These views are not rivals so much as layers, and the third has the advantage of explaining the exact shape of John's quotation. In every version the point is the same: Jesus is the righteous one the psalm describes, and He is also the lamb the Passover pictured. What should be resisted is any reading that treats the verse only as a disguised prediction and ignores its first meaning as a promise to every faithful sufferer.

debates.question: How much weight should the superscription about David at Gath carry when reading the psalm?

views.label: It is original and gives the setting
views.case: The superscription names the event, and 1 Samuel 21:10-15 supplies the details. Verses 4 to 6 fit a man who was afraid and saw God rescue him, and the psalm's praise reads more powerfully as coming from a man who had just acted the madman.

views.label: It is a later editorial note
views.case: The psalm never mentions Gath, madness or Achish, and its wisdom teaching in verses 11 to 22 has a general feel. On this view, later editors linked it to David because it suited his story, and the psalm should be read on its own terms.

views.label: The link is true, and the omission is the point
views.case: The psalm may be silent about the ruse because David wants all the credit to go to the LORD. Wisdom poems often leave their occasion in the background so that hearers can make the psalm their own.

debates.bearing: The psalm can be read profitably either way, since its language is broad enough to fit any poor man's cry. Taking the superscription seriously does add a sharp edge: it invites us to see that God's help can come to a person whose own conduct was less than glorious, and that David's response was to give the credit away.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 7 says the angel of the LORD 'encamps' around those who fear Him. The verb is chanah, to pitch camp, from the same root as machaneh, a camp or army. It is the word behind Mahanaim, the place where Jacob met 'the angels of God' and said, 'This is the camp of God', Genesis 32:1-2. The picture is of a pitched camp with the tents drawn up round the one being defended, and it lies close to what Elisha's servant saw when his eyes were opened to 'horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha', 2 Kings 6:17. The verb is a participle, so it describes something happening continuously and not a single rescue.

The word for refuge, chasah, comes twice in the psalm, 'blessed is the man who takes refuge in Him', verse 8, and 'none who take refuge in Him will be condemned', verse 22, so the psalm is bracketed by it. It is the verb of Psalm 2:12, 'Blessed are all who take refuge in Him', and of the image of the shadow of God's wings in Psalm 36:7 and Ruth 2:12. It pictures a person running to a shelter and staying there, not standing outside admiring it.

In verse 18 God is near to 'the brokenhearted', literally the 'broken of heart', from the same root as the bones that 'will not be broken' in verse 20. The psalm sets the two side by side. The heart may be shattered while the bones are kept whole, and the LORD is close to the one and guards the other. The 'contrite in spirit' next to them uses a word meaning 'crushed', and it is used in the same way in Isaiah 57:15, where the high and holy God dwells 'with the oppressed and humble in spirit', and in Isaiah 66:2, where He esteems 'he who is humble and contrite in spirit'.

The last two verses turn on a play of words. Verse 21 says the haters of the righteous 'will be condemned', and verse 22 says none who take refuge 'will be condemned'. The verb is asham, to be held guilty, from the family that also gives the word for guilt and for the guilt offering. Isaiah 53:10 uses the noun when the servant's life is made 'a guilt offering'. The psalm's last promise is that guilt will fall on one group and not on the other.

Finally, the word for 'redeems', padah, is used of buying back by payment or substitution, as with the firstborn that Israel redeemed, Exodus 13:13, and with God's rescue of His people from Egypt, Deuteronomy 7:8. Its use in the final line of an acrostic that has otherwise finished its alphabet gives the last word to God's costly rescue. A footnote worth knowing: the noun ta'am, related to the verb 'taste' in verse 8, is the word for the 'behavior' David changed before Achish in 1 Samuel 21:13, so the man who once altered his 'taste' to survive now invites others to taste for themselves.

typology.type: The unbroken bones of the Passover lamb, verse 20
typology.fulfillment: Israel was told not to break any of the bones of the Passover victim, Exodus 12:46 and Numbers 9:12, and John sees that regulation and this psalm meet at the cross, where the soldiers broke the legs of the two men beside Jesus but 'they did not break His legs', John 19:32-36. Paul says 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed', 1 Corinthians 5:7, and Peter that we were redeemed by the blood of 'a lamb without blemish or spot', 1 Peter 1:19. The type falls short in one respect: the lamb's whole bones showed that the sacrifice was unblemished, while Christ's whole bones sit beside a pierced side, John 19:34, and a death that the lamb could only picture.

typology.type: The poor man who cried and was heard, verse 6
typology.fulfillment: David is the poor man who called out and was heard, and the psalm treats him as an example for all the afflicted. Jesus is the poor man in the fullest sense, one who 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes became poor', 2 Corinthians 8:9, who was anointed to bring good news to the poor, Isaiah 61:1, and who 'offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears' and 'was heard because of His reverence', Hebrews 5:7. The pattern escalates because David was heard out of danger, while Jesus was heard through death, and raised, Acts 2:24.

typology.type: The camp of the angel of the LORD, verse 7
typology.fulfillment: The picture of angels encamped round the one who fears the LORD comes to a sharp point in Gethsemane, where Jesus tells Peter that He could call on the Father for 'more than twelve legions of angels', Matthew 26:53. The camp was there, and He did not summon it, because the rescue He had come to bring required the cross. The correspondence shows that God's protection is real, and the escalation shows that the greater deliverance sometimes needs the protection to be set aside. Hebrews adds that angels are 'ministering spirits' for the heirs of salvation, Hebrews 1:14.

typology.type: Many afflictions and deliverance out of them all, verse 19
typology.fulfillment: David's line, 'Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him from them all', has its final shape in the suffering and vindication of the one righteous man. Jesus was afflicted by betrayal, false accusation, abandonment and death, and 'God raised Him from the dead, releasing Him from the agony of death', Acts 2:24. His people follow the same path in smaller measure: Jesus tells them they will have trouble in this world, and calls them to take heart, John 16:33. The type falls short of the antitype because David was delivered from trouble, while Christ was delivered out of death itself.

study.christ:
John's reading of Psalm 34:20 is the most famous link, but it sits inside a larger set of ways the psalm leads to Jesus. The Fourth Gospel tells the scene with care. It was the day of Preparation, and the Jews asked Pilate to have the legs broken so the bodies would not remain on the crosses during the Sabbath, John 19:31. The soldiers broke the legs of the other two, but found Jesus already dead and did not break His. Then one of them pierced His side, and John, who is careful to say a witness saw it and that his testimony is true, gives two Scriptures for the double event: 'Not one of His bones will be broken', and 'They will look on the One they have pierced', John 19:36-37, from Zechariah 12:10. The pair matters. The psalm's promise of preserved bones is not a promise of a painless death. The Passover lamb had to be whole and slain, and here the true lamb is both.

The psalm also leads to Christ through the figure of the poor man. Verse 6, 'this poor man called out, and the LORD heard him', is picked up when Hebrews says Jesus 'offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard', Hebrews 5:7. Here the psalm's pattern of cry and answer is stretched to its limit. The answer is not rescue from death but rescue through it. When Jesus says 'Blessed are you who are poor', Luke 6:20, and when He announces good news to the poor, Isaiah 61:1, He is the one who stands with the psalm's poor because He has joined them, 2 Corinthians 8:9.

The psalm reaches Christ, third, by the way the New Testament handles the divine name. In verse 8 the LORD is the one to be tasted. Peter quotes the verse in 1 Peter 2:3 and, without any sense of strain, moves in the next verse to 'the living Stone', Christ, so that what was said of Yahweh is said of Jesus. Peter does the same in 1 Peter 3:12 with 'the eyes of the Lord'. This is not a trick with the word Lord. It is the apostolic conviction that what Israel found in the LORD is found in Christ.

Fourth, verse 22, 'The LORD redeems His servants', is where the psalm's final word meets the ransom Jesus paid, 'to give His life as a ransom for many', Mark 10:45. Peter says we were redeemed 'with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot', 1 Peter 1:19, linking the Passover lamb, whose unbroken bones the psalm remembers, with the redeeming work of verse 22.

A word of caution. Not every line of Psalm 34 is about Jesus, and the psalm is first the testimony of David and a lesson for the faithful. What the New Testament claims is that the righteous man the psalm describes is fully embodied in Christ, and that the psalm's promise of no condemnation, verse 22, comes true for those who take refuge in Him, Romans 8:1.
study.god:
Psalm 34 shows a God who is heard by being near. The verbs of the psalm are relational: He answered, verse 4, He heard, verses 6 and 17, He is near, verse 18. The God who is high enough for cherubim to camp round His people is also close enough to be 'near to the brokenhearted'. The psalm holds these together without embarrassment, and that is the first thing it teaches about God. Transcendence does not mean distance.

Second, God is good, and that goodness can be checked. 'Taste and see' is a remarkable invitation to make of a God who is elsewhere held up as beyond all testing. The claim is that His goodness has a flavour, that it is the kind of thing a person can find out by trying, and that the finding is dependable. The psalm never says that the taste will always be sweet in the mouth. It says the LORD is good, and that those who run to Him will lack nothing that is good, which is different from lacking nothing they want.

Third, God is morally serious. His ears are open to the righteous, and His face is set against those who do evil, 'to wipe out all memory of them from the earth', verse 16. Nearness to the humble and opposition to the wicked are two sides of one character. This is the God for whom truth in the tongue matters, verse 13, and for whom the desire to see good days is met with a demand to turn from evil, verses 12 and 14. He is not indifferent to how His people live.

Fourth, God is a redeemer who pays what redemption costs. The closing 'The LORD redeems His servants' does not describe a bystander who applauds those who escape. It describes one who acts to buy back. The psalm's claim that none who take refuge in Him will be condemned rests on that action, and the New Testament shows how costly it was.

The psalm also holds a tension it does not resolve. The LORD delivers 'from them all', yet the righteous suffer 'many' afflictions. He protects every bone, yet the faithful die. God's power and love are not in doubt, but the psalm does not promise an untroubled path. It promises His presence in the trouble and His verdict at the end.

For worship this means the psalm is a school in the right kind of praise. It blesses the LORD 'at all times', not only when circumstances are agreeable. It is a praise that can be sung by someone who has just been humiliated, because it rests on who God is and not on how things look. It calls the congregation to bring their own testimonies, to invite the oppressed to rejoice, to teach children the fear of the LORD, and to trust that the God who hears one poor man's cry hears the next.

crossReferences.note: The event named in the superscription: David, afraid before Achish king of Gath, changes his behavior and feigns madness. Reading the two together shows that the psalm's testimony of deliverance from 'all my fears' came from a moment of real terror and public humiliation, and that David credited the LORD rather than his own cleverness.

After Gath, David gathers at Adullam the distressed, the indebted and the discontented, four hundred of them. These are the poor and oppressed whom the psalm invites to hear and rejoice, verse 2, and a natural first audience for a poem that teaches the fear of the LORD.

Psalm 25 is another acrostic and ends, like Psalm 34, with an extra line beginning with pe: 'Redeem Israel, O God, from all its distress.' The shared closing word suggests both poems finish by asking or declaring that redemption belongs to the LORD.

The neighbouring psalm says the eyes of the LORD are on those who fear Him, 'to deliver them from death and keep them alive in famine'. Psalm 34:15 repeats the language of the LORD's eyes, and verse 10's promise of freedom from hunger echoes the famine line, turning a general truth into testimony.

The first psalms open with the blessing of the one who takes refuge in the LORD. Psalm 34 begins its invitation with the same word for blessed and ends its last verse with the same verb of refuge, so the poem quietly re-states the Psalter's opening promise from within a man's lived experience.

Jacob, meeting the angels of God on the road, says 'This is the camp of God' and names the place Mahanaim. It is the same root as the angel who 'encamps' in verse 7, and shows how old the idea is that God's people travel inside a guarded camp they cannot usually see.

Elisha's servant sees an enemy army and is afraid, until the LORD opens his eyes to horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha. It is a living picture of verse 7: the protection was already there before the servant could perceive it, and fear is answered by sight.

The high and holy One says He dwells with the oppressed and the humble in spirit, to revive the heart of the contrite. This is the same idea as verse 18, that God is nearest to those who are broken, and it shows the psalm taking up a theme the prophets would later develop.

Peter quotes verses 12 to 16 as counsel for Christians under pressure: guard the tongue, turn from evil, seek peace, because the Lord's eyes are on the righteous. He reads the psalm as instruction for suffering believers, not only for Israel's wise men, and grounds gentle conduct in God's attention.

John records that the soldiers did not break Jesus' legs and sets Psalm 34:20 beside the Passover law and the prophecy of the pierced One from Zechariah. The passage shows how the psalm's promise of protected bones is read as fulfilled in the death of the true Lamb.

Hebrews says Jesus offered loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death and was heard. It gives the psalm's picture of the poor man who cries and is heard its deepest instance, and shows that being heard can mean being carried through death.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story of taste begins badly. In the garden 'the woman saw that the tree was good for food and pleasing to the eyes', and 'she took the fruit and ate it', Genesis 3:6. Seeing, tasting and judging something good, apart from God's word, is the first act of human independence. Psalm 34:8 invites the same three senses to a better use: 'Taste and see that the LORD is good.' What was ruined by eating the forbidden fruit is offered again as a meal to which God invites His people, and the goodness they judge is God's own. The psalm is one of many small places where the Bible quietly heals the story of Genesis 3.

Between the garden and the new creation the psalm sits in the story of a rescued and hunted people. Israel's founding rescue was the Passover, and the bone regulation belongs to that night. David, anointed but running for his life, is a small Israel in exile, saved from a foreign king by a rescue he could not claim as his own, and gathering the distressed round him. The psalm becomes a song for exile, sung by people who have to live well while the world is against them, which is why Peter can hand it to Christians who are foreigners and exiles, 1 Peter 2:11.

The story comes to its centre in Jesus. The Passover lamb whose bones were not broken is the one who was pierced for us, and the poor man who cried and was heard is the one whom God raised. He fulfils the psalm's promises, 'not one of them will be broken', 'none who take refuge in Him will be condemned', in the way that matters most: for His people, condemnation is gone, Romans 8:1, and their afflictions, though real, do not have the last word, Acts 14:22 and Romans 8:35-39.

The end of the story is the psalm's promises kept in full. 'Those who fear Him lack nothing' becomes 'Never again will they hunger, and never will they thirst', Revelation 7:16, and 'God will wipe away every tear from their eyes', Revelation 7:17. 'Their faces shall never be ashamed' becomes 'They will see His face', Revelation 22:4. The children who were taught the fear of the LORD are gathered into a family that will never be broken. The song begun in a cave by a man in trouble is finished by a multitude who have tasted, and seen, and are satisfied.

sermon.title: "This Poor Man Cried"
sermon.why: Begg's meditation on Psalm 34:6 shows that pride keeps us from bringing our troubles humbly to the Lord, and that when we earnestly and humbly call on Christ, following David's example, He hears us and answers.

quiz.q: What does David resolve to do in verse 1?

options.text: Bless the LORD at all times, with His praise always on his lips.
options.note: This opening resolution sets the tone for the whole psalm's ongoing, not merely occasional, praise.

options.text: Praise the LORD only after every trouble ends.
options.note: The resolution is to praise at all times, not to wait until difficulty passes.

options.text: Praise the LORD often, but only when he personally feels like it.
options.note: Close, since frequent praise is right, but verse 1 commits to praise 'at all times,' regardless of feeling, not conditioned on his mood.

options.text: Praise the LORD only in the temple.
options.note: The resolution is for continual, all-times praise, not limited to a specific location.

quiz.q: What invitation does David extend in verse 8?

options.text: Taste and see that the LORD is good.
options.note: This is the psalm's central, most quoted invitation to experience God's goodness directly.

options.text: Believe correct facts about God's goodness without necessarily experiencing it.
options.note: Close, since right belief matters, but 'taste and see' specifically calls for direct, personal experience, not mere intellectual assent to facts.

options.text: Judge whether the LORD is good based on others' testimony alone.
options.note: The invitation is to personal, direct experience, tasting and seeing, not secondhand testimony alone.

options.text: Wait until death to know if God is good.
options.note: The invitation is for present, immediate experience of God's goodness.

quiz.q: What does David teach children in verses 11-14?

options.text: The fear of the LORD, including keeping the tongue from evil and turning from evil to do good.
options.note: This section is explicit wisdom instruction aimed at the next generation.

options.text: General good manners toward others.
options.note: Close, since kind conduct is part of the teaching, but the instruction is specifically rooted in the fear of the LORD, not manners considered apart from reverence for God.

options.text: How to acquire wealth quickly.
options.note: The teaching concerns the fear of the LORD and righteous speech and conduct, not wealth acquisition.

options.text: How to avoid ever speaking to anyone.
options.note: The instruction is about controlling speech to avoid evil and deceit, not avoiding speech altogether.

quiz.q: According to verse 18, where is the LORD especially near?

options.text: To the brokenhearted, saving the contrite in spirit.
options.note: This verse specifically identifies God's nearness to those crushed in spirit.

options.text: To all people equally, regardless of their emotional or spiritual state.
options.note: Close, since God's care extends broadly, but verse 18 specifically highlights a special nearness to the brokenhearted and contrite, not an undifferentiated nearness to everyone.

options.text: Only to kings and rulers.
options.note: The nearness described is to the brokenhearted broadly, not limited to political leaders.

options.text: Nowhere in particular; God is equally distant from all.
options.note: This is the opposite of the verse's claim about God's special nearness to the brokenhearted.

quiz.q: What promise does verse 20 make, and where is it quoted as fulfilled in the New Testament?

options.text: That not one of the righteous person's bones will be broken, quoted as fulfilled at the crucifixion in John 19:36.
options.note: John explicitly connects this promise to the soldiers not breaking Jesus's legs at the cross.

options.text: That the righteous will be kept safe from serious harm, referenced generally in the Gospels.
options.note: Close, since safety is the broader theme, but the specific promise concerns bones not being broken, and its precise New Testament quotation is in John 19:36, not a general Gospel reference.

options.text: That the wicked will have their bones broken as punishment, quoted in Romans.
options.note: The verse's promise concerns protection of the righteous, not judgment on the wicked, and its New Testament quotation is in John's Gospel.

options.text: That believers will be physically immortal in this life.
options.note: The promise is specifically about bones not being broken, not general immortality in this present life.

questions: David resolves to bless the LORD at all times, not only when circumstances are good. What would it look like for you to praise God specifically in whatever difficulty you are facing right now?

David invites others to taste and see that the LORD is good, an experiential knowledge, not mere information. Where in your life have you settled for knowing facts about God rather than genuinely tasting His goodness?

David teaches children to keep their tongue from evil and deceit, and to seek peace and pursue it. What would it look like for you to actively pursue peace this week rather than simply avoiding open conflict?

The psalm says the LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the contrite in spirit. Where are you brokenhearted right now, and how does knowing God draws especially near in that state change how you bring it to Him?

John shows this psalm's promise of unbroken bones fulfilled at the cross, connecting Jesus to the Passover Lamb. How does seeing Christ as the true Passover Lamb, sacrificed for you, deepen your understanding of the deliverance this psalm celebrates?

translationNotes.note: This poor man likely refers to David himself, using the term ani, poor or afflicted, as an honest description of his condition when he cried out and was heard.
Taste and see renders taam, to perceive by direct experience, quoted by Peter in 1 Peter 2:3 to describe believers' experiential knowledge of Christ's goodness.
Not one of them will be broken is quoted directly in John 19:36 as fulfilled at the crucifixion, and echoes the Passover lamb regulation of Exodus 12:46 that no bone of the lamb be broken.
